sections.h2: What should I know before selling a house in Middletown Township?
sections.html:
Middletown Township in Bucks County requires a Level 2 chimney inspection on every home that is sold, and Levittown sections add a heater compartment wall inspection. That fire marshal rule is the main local step, followed by a 2 percent transfer tax paid at recording.

The township has 46,040 residents, according to the 2020 census, spread across about 19 square miles in the Philadelphia metropolitan area. It surrounds the boroughs of Langhorne, Langhorne Manor, Penndel and Hulmeville, which is why many addresses read Langhorne even though they sit in the township. Do not confuse it with other Pennsylvania townships that share the Middletown name; this page covers the Bucks County one only.

Sellers can list, sell without an agent or accept a cash purchase. The township rules below apply whichever route you choose.

sections.h2: How did Levittown shape Middletown Township?
sections.html:
The township was formally established in 1692 and stayed farmland for most of its history. In 1930 it had only 2,095 residents, and in 1950 it had 4,987. Then William Levitt began his second Levittown, which reached into four municipalities including Middletown, and the 1960 census counted 26,936 people, a 440 percent jump.

That history explains the housing mix you will find on a listing search:

  • Levittown sections in the south, built in the 1950s, with hundreds of similar homes per development.
  • Parkland, where houses date from every decade of the 20th century and the 21st.
  • Newer townhouses and condominiums around the Oxford Valley Mall, along with assisted living and 55-plus housing.
  • A few older farm properties; Edgemont, Harewood and Beechwood carry National Register listings.

The township later preserved hundreds of acres, now Core Creek Park with Lake Luxembourg, and saved Styer's Orchards from a plan for 632 homes in the late 1990s. Sesame Place and part of Cairn University are also inside the township.

sections.h2: What inspection does Middletown Township require when a house sells?
sections.html:
Every home sold in the township needs a Level 2 chimney inspection, and the Fire and Emergency Management office keeps a copy. The rule follows NFPA 211, which calls for the inspection any time a property is sold or transferred.

The inspection covers any appliance that vents combustion gases, including oil-fired and gas-fired heaters with a metal B-vent chimney, fireplaces, wood stoves and pellet stoves. A certified CSIA chimney sweep must do it, and the township website keeps a courtesy list of local sweeps. The requirement does not apply to a home heated and cooled only by electric devices or one with a vent-less fireplace, and plastic PVC exhaust pipe does not need a Level 2 inspection.

sections.h2: How much are property taxes in Middletown Township?
sections.html:
The 2026 combined millage in Middletown Township is 252.2674 mills, according to the Bucks County millage list effective July 1, 2026. Three taxing bodies make up that number: the county at 29.65 mills, the Neshaminy School District at 198.0124 mills and the township at 24.605 mills.

The township's own 24.605 mills break down into a general fund of 7.025, a debt service fund of 5.115, fire protection of 4.75, parks and recreation of 3.25 and fire apparatus of 2.5, plus smaller street light, ambulance, road machinery and hydrant levies. One mill equals a dollar of tax on each thousand dollars of assessment. The Bucks County Board of Assessment sets each property's assessed value.

Because Neshaminy carries most of the load, the school district millage drives the difference between Middletown and nearby municipalities in other districts. For comparison, the same county list shows Falls Township at 250.763 total mills and Lower Makefield at 265.786.

sections.h2: What is the transfer tax on a Middletown sale?
sections.html:
The Bucks County Recorder of Deeds describes a 2 percent transfer tax on property sales in Pennsylvania, with 1 percent to the state and 1 percent to the municipality and school district. Payment is made at recording, and the value that is taxed can differ from the sales price.

Neither state nor local government says who pays, and in most agreements the buyer and seller divide it. The new owner is responsible if the amount paid turns out to be wrong. Starting in January 2026, the recorder's office stopped accepting personal checks for the tax. Payment options are cash in the office, cashier's check, money order or credit card, so tell your title company early.

  • Transfers between spouses, parents and children, grandparents and grandchildren, and siblings can be exempt.
  • A one-time transfer between former spouses is allowed.
  • A $1 deed or a transfer with no tax paid needs a statement of value so state investigators can check the real worth.

The recorder's office can be reached at 215-348-6209 for exemption questions.

sections.h2: When can I appeal a Bucks County assessment?
sections.html:
The 2026 annual appeal deadline was August 3, and it has passed. Any change from that cycle takes effect for the 2027 tax year.

The Board of Assessment Appeals sits at 55 East Court Street in Doylestown and can be reached at 215-348-6219. It meets at 10 a.m. on the first and third Tuesdays of each month. Appeal forms and rules for both residential and commercial properties are posted on the county site.

Two other county items apply to sellers and buyers. The homestead and farmstead exclusion application is due March 1 for the tax year beginning the following July 1, and a new owner must give the Board of Assessment contact information within 30 days of buying, under Act 29.

sections.h2: What affects a Middletown Township house's value and appeal?
sections.html:
Location along the Philadelphia and Trenton corridor, school assignments and weather exposure all shape buyer interest. Interstate 295 runs through the east side of the township, and U.S. Route 1 crosses the middle. Pennsylvania routes 213, 413, 332 and 513 also touch it. The township reports 189.70 miles of public roads, of which the township maintains 139.07 miles.

SEPTA's West Trenton Regional Rail line stops at Woodbourne station in the township, and Langhorne station is just across the line in Langhorne Manor. SEPTA also runs City Bus route 14 and suburban routes 127, 128, 129 and 130 through the area.

Neshaminy School District serves the township. Albert Schweitzer, Herbert Hoover, Pearl S. Buck, Tawanka and Walter Miller elementary schools cover kindergarten through fourth grade, Carl Sandburg and Maple Point middle schools take grades five through eight, and Neshaminy High School serves grades nine through twelve.

NOAA's 1991 to 2020 normals for the Neshaminy Falls station show 50.7 inches of rain and melted snow per year plus 19.9 inches of snowfall, and July is the wettest month. The township record wet day was 6.60 inches on August 27, 2011, so basements and drainage are a fair question for any buyer inspection.

sections.h2: Is a listing or a cash sale the better fit in Middletown?
sections.html:
A cash sale suits a property with deferred repairs, while a listing suits one a lender will finance as it stands. Either way, the chimney inspection comes first, and a failed inspection can change what you can ask.

  • Book a CSIA chimney sweep before you list and send the report to the fire marshal.
  • If the house is in Levittown, ask the fire office what the heater compartment wall inspection involves.
  • Compare offers after the 2 percent transfer tax, your mortgage payoff and the school and township tax proration.

faqs.q: Does Middletown Township require a chimney inspection when I sell?
faqs.a: Yes. A Level 2 chimney inspection by a certified CSIA sweep is required for homes with combustion appliances, and a copy goes to Fire and Emergency Management. Levittown homes also need a heater compartment wall inspection.

faqs.q: What is the transfer tax in Middletown Township?
faqs.a: The Bucks County Recorder of Deeds lists 2 percent in total: 1 percent to the state and 1 percent to the municipality and school district. The tax is paid at the time of recording.

faqs.q: Which school district serves Middletown Township?
faqs.a: Neshaminy School District. Five elementary schools, two middle schools and Neshaminy High School serve the township.

faqs.q: What is the total property tax rate in Middletown Township?
faqs.a: The county's July 1, 2026 list shows 252.2674 mills combined: 29.65 for the county, 198.0124 for Neshaminy School District and 24.605 for the township.

faqs.q: Can I still file a Bucks County assessment appeal for 2026?
faqs.a: No. The 2026 annual appeal deadline was August 3, 2026, and it has passed. Call the Board of Assessment at 215-348-6219 to ask about the next annual cycle.
